newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS-Nordic steel firms see higher earnings,prices.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Nordic steel firms see higher earnings,prices.

text.p: Nordic steel companies painted a rosier picture for their future earnings on Thursday and analysts said an upturn in steel prices lay ahead in the second half of the year.
"Prices should come up in the second half of 1997, but there won't be a surge, rather single digit percent figures," Gustav Lucander, analyst at Aros Securities in Helsinki, told Reuters.
Swedish steel company SSAB, Finnish rival Rautaruukki and Swedish-British group Avesta Sheffield reported lower earnings on Thursday due to a weak market with lower steel prices.

Carbon steel maker SSAB showed a 45 percent drop in 1996 profit after financial items to 2.09 billion crowns ($282.5 million), while competitor Rautaruukki posted a profit before extraordinary items and tax of 715 million markka ($144 million) last year, down 25 percent.

Stainless steel manufacturer Avesta Sheffield plunged into the red in the first nine months of its fiscal year 1996-1997, reporting a pretax loss of 136 million crowns, compared with a pretax profit of 3.15 billion.
SSAB and Rautaruukki beat analysts' estimates of 1.98 billion crowns and 660 million markka, respectively, while Avesta did not meet expectations of a 163 million crown profit.
Avesta partly pointed to delays in starting up new plants, the stronger crown and pound, a lower value of its raw materials stocks and costs for phasing out a Baltimore plant.
But all three expressed cautious optimism about the future.

"Rautaruukki's earnings are estimated to be better than in 1996 provided that the trend in the steel market develops as forecast," the company said, adding that the steel product prices were expected to be higher in 1997.
SSAB said its future earnings would hinge on steel prices and analysts agreed.
"SSAB's earnings completely depend on steel prices as it operates at full capacity," said Christofer Sjogren, analyst at Carnegie brokerage in Stockholm.

Although SSAB said it could not see any substantial signs of a recovery in steel demand in Western Europe, it said several experts expected demand to increase in 1997, partly as they did not see any further decrease in stocks.
Analysts said SSAB's report breathed some optimism into the industry and Avesta Sheffield was outspoken about a future market upturn.
"Price increases are announced and we think they will go through," Adri De Ridder at Avesta Sheffield's investor relations told Reuters.
Two important producers, the German group Krupp Thyssen Nirosta and Acerinox, have announced price increases, mainly on some cold rolled products. Avesta would follow suit, De Ridder said.
But unlike carbon steel makers SSAB and Rautaruukki, Avesta is dependant on nickel and chrome prices, which apart from carbon steel, are parts of stainless steel.
"Nickel and chrome are traded on the market and their prices swing sharply. Therefore Avesta's earnings can go through the floor or surge to the sky," an analyst said.
But overcapacity could be lurking in both the carbon steel and stainless steel markets, analysts said.
"There is a risk of overcapacity as companies could step on it when things look brighter, but if you have a positive view about European demand keeping up, prices should rise," Lucander said.
-- Stockholm newsroom +46-8-700 1006 ($ = 7.397 Swedish Crowns) ($ = 4.966 Finnish Markka)
